chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub from Jameel ibn Salih from Abu Ubayda al-Hadda' who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who struck a man with a tent pole on his head with one strike, causing it to pierce to the brain, so his intellect was lost. He (peace be upon him) said: If the struck one does not comprehend the prayer from it, nor comprehend what he says, nor what is said to him, then he is awaited for a year. If he dies in the period between the strike and the year, the striker is retaliated with (qisas); and if he does not die in that period and his intellect does not return to him, the striker is liable for the blood money (diyah) from his wealth due to the loss of his intellect.

I said to him, 'So what do you view upon him for the fracture?' He said, 'No, because he struck him with one strike, so the one strike committed two crimes. Therefore, I hold him liable for the harshest of the two crimes, which is the blood money. And if he had struck him with two strikes, so the two strikes committed two crimes, I would hold him liable for the crime of what they committed, whatever they were, except if death occurs in them, then the striker is retaliated with (qisas).' [Note: The phrase 'بِوَاحِدَةٍ وَ تُطْرَحَ الْأُخْرَى' is implied in the context of qisas vs diyah for multiple strikes where one causes death, though the text provided in the prompt's Arabic block for this specific segment ends at 'ضَارِبُهُ'. The prompt's Arabic text for this chunk is: 'قُلْتُ لَهُ فَمَا تَرَى عَلَيْهِ فِي الشَّجَّةِ شَيْئاً قَالَ لَا لِأَنَّهُ إِنَّمَا ضَرَبَهُ ضَرْبَةً وَاحِدَةً فَجَنَتِ الضَّرْبَةُ جِنَايَتَيْنِ فَأُلْزِمُهُ أَغْلَظَ الْجِنَايَتَيْنِ وَ هِيَ الدِّيَةُ وَ لَوْ كَانَ ضَرَبَهُ ضَرْبَتَيْنِ فَجَنَتِ الضَّرْبَتَانِ جِنَايَتَيْنِ لَأَلْزَمْتُهُ جِنَايَةَ مَا جَنَتَا كَانَتَا مَا كَانَتَا إِلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ فِيهِمَا الْمَوْتُ فَيُقَادَ بِهِ ضَارِبُهُ']

He said, 'And he said: If he struck him with three strikes, one after another, so they committed three crimes, I would hold him liable for the crime of what the three strikes committed, whatever they were, as long as death is not in them, then the striker is retaliated with.'
He said, 'And he said: If he struck him with ten strikes, so they committed one crime, I would hold him liable for that one crime which the ten strikes committed, whatever it was.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on compensation for a head injury that causes permanent loss of intellect?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the jurisprudential principles of *diyah* (blood money) and *qisas* (retaliation) regarding head injuries that impair intellect, specifically addressing the 'year of waiting' (*sanat al-intizar*) to determine if the injury is permanent. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that for a single strike causing multiple damages, the most severe penalty applies, whereas multiple strikes incur cumulative liability unless death occurs, illustrating the Shia legal distinction between singular and plural causation in bodily harm. This ruling underscores the precision of Imami jurisprudence in distinguishing between temporary and permanent loss of faculties, a key topic in *fiqh al-jaraha*.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, and Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Jameel Bin Salih, from Abu Ubeyda Al Haza’a who said,

‘I asked Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> about a man who struck a man with a pole of a tent, upon his head, with one strike. So it pierced him to the extent that it arrived to the brain. So his intellect went’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If it was that the struck one did not have the intellect for the Prayer, nor any intellect of what he says, nor what is said to him, so he would be awaited with for a year. So if he were to dies in what is between it and the year, his striker would be retaliated with; and if he does not die in what is between it and the year, and his intellect does not return to him, his striker would be fined the (complete) wergild in his wealth, due to the going away of his (victim’s) intellect.

I said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘So what do you<sup>asws</sup> view to be upon him for fracturing something?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘No, because, rather he struck him with one strike. So the one strike committed two crimes. Therefore, it necessitates him the harshest of the two crimes, and it is the (complete) wergild. And had he struck him with two strikes, so the two strikes would have committed two crimes, it would necessitate him one crime, so whatever was it was, except if there happens to be the death in it, so his striker would be retaliated (due to one strike and the other would be dropped).

So if he had struck him with three stroked, one after the other, so he would have committed three crimes, it would necessitate him with one crime what the three strikes had committed, as it if was such, for as long as there does not happen to be the death in it, so his striker would be retaliated with.
So if he had struck him with ten strike, so it would be the one crime, even it ten strikes had committed, so he will be held for one crime – whatever it may be’.
